recentItems.title: The Good, the Baddies, and the Ugly
recentItems.description:
Are we living in a Baddies Revolution?

We just might be. Over the past few years, the Zeus Network franchise Baddies has steadily grown in virality, capturing dozens of young people on camera as they party, promote clubs, and most of all, fight each other. But where do shows like Joseline's Cabaret and Baddies USA sit in the long history of Reality TV, and what can they tell us about what young people feel is possible for themselves? To find out,  Brittany is joined by Dr. Donnetrice C. Allison (https://www.linkedin.com/in/donnetrice-allison-ph-d-743080298/) , professor and chair of the department of Africana studies at Stockton University.

Want more conversations at the intersection of labor and entertainment? Check out theses episodes:

Would you let your kids play football? (https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-5962179/would-you-let-your-kids-play-football) 
Has Broadway lost its way? (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/19/nx-s1-5936555/has-broadway-lost-its-way)

recentItems.title: Katherine Rundell says it's a mistake for adults to discard children's literature
recentItems.description:
Katherine Rundell’s Impossible Creatures series follows two kid heroes on their journey to save a group of islands filled with magical beasts. She’s the first children's author since J.K. Rowling to simultaneously top the U.K. and U.S. sales charts. Now, Rundell is out with The Neverfear, the third installment in the series. She’s also authored a book-length essay called Why You Should Read Children's Books, Even Though You Are So Old and Wise. In today’s episode, she talks with Here & Now’s Indira Lakshmanan about how children’s literature gets to “the meat of the human heart.”

recentItems.title: Your summer (Sponsored by prediction markets)
recentItems.description: The summer of 2026 turned into the summer of predictive markets. Polymarket and Kalshi, two of the largest betting platforms in the US, expanded their marketing to reach users everywhere. And they seem to be actively pursuing women customers — highlighting bets on who'd win Love Island USA to who'd attend the Taylor Swift Travis Kelce wedding. To discuss this phenomenon, we’re talking with Nancy Walecki (@nancywalecki.bsky.social), staff writer at The Atlantic and Lauren McCarthy (@laurenmccarth), business reporter at The New York Times, to understand how predictive markets are catering to women, and what it all means.

recentItems.title: Why can’t people be normal about the WNBA? | Code Switch
recentItems.description:
The WNBA is more popular than ever, but the growth has come with a lot of unwanted attention, like protests at games and death threats directed towards players. This week, we talk with independent journalist Frankie de la Cretaz about what brought all of this hate into the league, and NPR’s domestic extremism correspondent, Odette Yousef, about the ways the league is responding.

recentItems.title: 'Odyssey' translator Emily Wilson on her book of essays 'Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea'
recentItems.description:
Emily Wilson is a classicist whose translations of The Iliad and The Odyssey are popular and controversial. Recently, she was at the center of the discourse surrounding Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of The Odyssey. Her new book of essays reflects on translation and the role of classics in modern society. In it, she argues that "it is a waste of everyone's time if a retranslation takes more or less the same approach as one or more existing published translations." In today’s episode, she speaks with NPR’s Joel Rose about Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea.

recentItems.title: Marlon James' novel 'The Disappearers' chronicles the aftermath of a violent attack
recentItems.description:
In 1988, a group of gay men gathered in Kingston, Jamaica to put on a play. At the time, homophobia in the country was rampant and sex between men was outlawed. Marlon James’ new novel The Disappearers is about a hateful mob attack at one of the group’s rehearsals. In an interview with All Things Considered’s Juana Summers, James said “this attack in the book was based on an incident which I knew in my gut happened. I just couldn’t prove it.” In today’s episode, Summers and James discuss the untrustworthy quality of official records and the author’s views on writing about violence.

recentItems.title: The rising power of American Muslims | It's Been a Minute
recentItems.description:
Is this a new era for American Muslims?

American Muslims are building their own cultural institutions – New York Magazine (https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/swana-new-york.html)  and The Guardian (https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/feb/03/muslim-new-york-city)  have reported on flourishing ecosystems of cafes, magazines, dance nights, meetups and readings for Muslims and/or people with heritage from the SWANA region. And on a political level, Muslims like Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani have become prominent faces of the left. On the one hand, this swell of Muslims coming up in politics and building cultural institutions is not surprising – there are over 4 million Muslims in America. On the other hand, this shift is pretty significant given how deeply Islamophobia and racism are rooted in our culture. So what's changed for American Muslims in recent years, and what’s stayed the same? What does it mean that Muslims are accruing a little more political and cultural capital now, and that non-Muslims are noticing?

To get deeper into it, Brittany is joined by Dr. Donna Auston (https://donnaauston.com/about/) , cultural anthropologist, and Dr. Tazeen Ali (https://rap.wustl.edu/people/tazeen-ali/) , scholar of Islam in America and associate professor of religion and politics at Washington University in St. Louis.

(00:00) Is this a new era for American Muslims?
(02:19) From family joints to Instagrammable coffee shops
(11:11) The Muslim faces of the progressive movement
(14:51) Systemic Islamophobia in America
(20:35) How race shapes Muslim communities
(27:04) Shifting views on Gaza amidst persistent Islamophobia

recentItems.title: English language programs are in crisis
recentItems.description:
Last year, President Trump made English the official language of the United States. Then his administration move to zero out the federal budget for teaching English. But even when those programs were fully funded, they reached fewer then 5% of the 25 million adults in the country still learning English.

Code Switch producer Xavier Lopez talks with author Kai Kalia Yang about the language needs of her Hmong community in Minnesota.

recentItems.title: Why we’re all being watched | Code Switch
recentItems.description:
There’s a growing backlash to the surveillance systems that have quietly wired themselves into American neighborhoods, with concern growing among people who have never felt watched this way before. Gene talks with historian Matthew Guariglia about how the surveillance state got built, who it was built on first, and why opposing it now unites so many factions.

recentItems.title: The manosphere is coming for R&B | It's Been A Minute
recentItems.description:
The genre made for lovers doesn't seem to respect the very fanbase it’s engineered to woo.

When Mankaprr Conteh (https://www.instagram.com/mankaprr/?hl=en)  interviewed R&B artist Isaia Huron, she imagined a thoughtful if not a bit complicated conversation about the difficult woman at the center of his latest album, Mr. Lovebomb. What she got was something else entirely.

Huron went on to tell Mankaprr that he has no empathy for women and that it's problematic that women believe they deserve everything. This conversation was later turned into Mankaprr’s piece for Hammer & Hope magazine: “Is This What R&B Sounds Like When You Don’t Respect Women?” (https://hammerandhope.org/article/isaia-huron-manosphere)  Huron’s casual misogyny in a genre like R&B raised more questions than answers.

Today on the show, journalist and 2026–2027 Knight-Wallace Arts Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan Mankaprr Conteh, joins Brittany to break down Huron’s surprising comments, ‘vibes based chauvinism,’ and the state of R&B today.

recentItems.title: Marking 25 years since Sept. 11 with 'All the Presidents' Wars' and 'Scattered Steel'
recentItems.description:
On today’s show, we mark the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11 with two books that historicize the attacks. First, All the Presidents’ Wars focuses on anti-terror campaigns waged around the world over the past quarter century. Author Peter Bergen spoke with Morning Edition’s Steve Inskeep about the expansion of executive branch powers that have enabled these wars. Then, Scattered Steel investigates how material from the World Trade Center ended up in memorials across the country. All Things Considered’s Scott Detrow spoke with Sam Holleran – who co-authored the book with his brother, Max Holleran.
